862.title: Parents as they are
862.hook: honor thy father and thy mother (Exodus 20:12), with honest boundaries
862.howItsDone: Jews and Christians count honoring parents among the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in concrete acts of care; in Confucian tradition filial respect is central, and families honor elders through visits, care and remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Emerson: the only way to have a friend is to be one. Your line was tend it.

A grown woman pulls into her parents' driveway and sits in the car for a minute before going in. Engine off. Hands on the wheel. Inside is the man who taught her to ride a bike, and who still knows exactly which comment will make her feel twelve years old. She loves him. She's also bracing. Both are true at once, and neither cancels the other. Ancient law codes, sages and scriptures all speak about parents: what honoring them asks, and what it doesn't.
screen: `SITTING IN THE CAR FOR A MINUTE.` → `LOVING AND BRACING AT ONCE.` → `WHAT HONOR ASKS, AND DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: First, the commandment. Among the Ten Commandments in Exodus: "Honour thy father and thy mother." It doesn't say love them warmly at every moment, or agree with them, or pretend they were perfect. It says honor. Second, honor is actions. The rabbis of the Talmud asked what honoring a parent looks like, and their answers are concrete: providing food and drink, clothing, helping them come and go. Reverence, they said, means things like not standing or sitting in a parent's place and not contradicting their words. Honor is something you do, whatever you happen to feel that afternoon. Third, Confucius on support. In the Analects, Confucius notes that in his day filial duty is taken to mean simply feeding your parents. But dogs and horses get fed too, he says. Without respect, what's the difference? Elsewhere he says a child may disagree with a parent, but gently. Even in a tradition that places parents very high, honest disagreement has a place. Fourth, honor with boundaries. Leviticus pairs two commands in one breath: "Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father, and keep my sabbaths." The rabbis read that pairing as a limit: if a parent tells a child to break the sabbath, the child doesn't obey, because parent and child both answer to God. Honor has edges. For people whose parents caused real harm, some teachers say honor can mean decency kept at a safe distance. Parents as they are: not as we wish they were, and not more than they are either.

segments.voice: Let a parent, a grandparent or an elder who raised you come to mind; if they've died, remembering is a form of honor too. See them as they are or were, their age, their tiredness, the history they carried, and let one thing they gave you sit beside one boundary you need with them, without the two arguing. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name.

Your line: as they are. Honor can be a full plate, a gentle word, or decency at a safe distance. See you tomorrow.

863.title: Loving children
863.hook: Gibran: your children come through you but are not from you (The Prophet, 1923)
863.howItsDone: Gibran's chapter 'On Children' is read aloud by some families and at some ceremonies; Christians tell the story of the boy Jesus in the temple from Luke 2.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kabed: honor, shown in acts of care. Your line was as they are.

On the inside of a kitchen doorframe, a column of pencil lines climbs toward the ceiling, each with a name and a date. Somebody stood very straight in socks while somebody else laid a book flat on their head. The lines are a record of growth, and of something harder: every one marks a child getting a little further from needing the person holding the pencil. A Lebanese-American poet wrote a short chapter about exactly that, and an older story says it without saying it.
screen: `PENCIL LINES ON A DOORFRAME.` → `A RECORD OF GROWING AWAY.` → `A POET AND AN OLDER STORY.`

segments.voice: First, not your children. In Kahlil Gibran's book The Prophet, a woman holding a baby asks the prophet to speak of children. His first words are startling: "Your children are not your children." He goes on: "They are the sons and daughters of Life's longing for itself." It sounds cold at first. It isn't. A child is bigger than the plans anyone makes for them. Second, through you, not from you. "They come through you but not from you," the prophet says. A parent is a doorway, not an owner. And then: "You may give them your love but not your thoughts, For they have their own thoughts." A child's inner life is their own. Third, the bow and the arrow. "You are the bows from which your children as living arrows are sent forth." Gibran ends by asking the bow to bend gladly in the archer's hand, because the archer loves the bow that stays steady as much as the arrow that flies. The parent isn't sidelined; the parent makes the flight possible. Fourth, a mother keeps it in her heart. In the Gospel of Luke, the boy Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents search for him for days. When they find him, Mary says: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." The text says they didn't understand his answer. And then, simply: "his mother kept all these sayings in her heart." She keeps his words without needing to master them.

segments.voice: Let a child come to mind, your own, a niece, a student, a neighbor's kid, or the child you once were, and see them as they actually are right now: what they love, what makes them laugh. Notice one way they're different from what anyone expected, and instead of correcting it, let it be, and quietly wish them well in it, steady as the bow. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name.

Your line: through you, not from you. The bow sends; the arrow flies. Day eight hundred sixty-three.

864.title: Loving strangers
864.hook: in several traditions, the stranger is a test of love
864.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Abraham's welcome of three guests in Genesis 18 as a model of hospitality, and the Torah commands love for the stranger; hospitality to guests and travelers is also honored in other faiths and cultures.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was loving children: love that gives freely and holds loosely. Your line was through you, not from you.

Who was the last stranger to do something kind for you? Someone who held a door with a foot while juggling groceries. A driver who waved you into traffic. A person on a train who pointed out that your bag was open. They may never turn up again, and they didn't need anything back. Strangers are the people love has the least reason to reach: no history, no debt, no family tie. That's exactly why several ancient texts made the stranger a test.
screen: `THE LAST STRANGER WHO WAS KIND.` → `NO HISTORY, NO DEBT.` → `WHY THE STRANGER IS A TEST.`

segments.voice: First, Abraham runs to the strangers. In Genesis, Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day when he sees three men standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows, and asks them to stay. Then he hurries: water for their feet, fresh bread, a calf prepared, food set before them while he stands by. The chapter opens by telling the reader that the LORD appeared to Abraham there; how much Abraham himself understood at first, the text leaves open. Second, ye were strangers. Leviticus doesn't just say tolerate the outsider: "thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The reason given is memory. You know what it's like to be the outsider. Third, angels unawares. The letter to the Hebrews has a line in which some readers hear Abraham's story: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." The Greeks had their own version: in Homer's Odyssey, a princess tells her frightened friends that strangers and beggars come from Zeus. Fourth, a smile is small hospitality. Not everyone has a tent or a calf to offer. But hospitality comes in small sizes: eye contact with the cashier, patience with a lost tourist, a nod to the new person at work. These texts treat the stranger not as a risk to manage but as someone to welcome, with common sense about safety. Here, the stranger is where love reaches past loyalty.

segments.voice: Let a stranger who once did something kind for you come back to mind, a door held, a wave into traffic, directions on a strange street, and stay with that moment for a few breaths. Let the thanks you never got to say be said silently now. If you pray, you can give thanks for that stranger before God, nameless as they are.
Loving strangers. Welcome offered to people with no claim on you, the way Abraham ran to his guests and Leviticus says to love the outsider as yourself. Today's word.
Your line: the stranger. Every one of us has been the outsider somewhere. Until tomorrow.

865.title: Loving animals
865.hook: Francis preaches to the birds (Little Flowers 16); Buddhists and Jains stress not harming
865.howItsDone: Some Catholic and other Christian churches hold a blessing of animals on Saint Francis's feast day; Jains practice ahimsa toward all living beings, and some Jain monks and nuns sweep their path to avoid harming insects; Buddhists take a precept to refrain from harming living beings.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was loving strangers: welcome for people with no claim on you. Your line was the stranger.

A man in a rough patched habit is walking along a road in Italy with his companions when he notices trees full of birds and a field full of more. He tells his friends to wait. Then he walks into the field and starts preaching. To the birds. The story says they don't scatter. They stay, and listen, and don't fly off until he gives them his blessing. It's one of the stories gathered in The Little Flowers of Saint Francis, and it could be read as a charming legend and nothing more.
screen: `A FIELD FULL OF BIRDS.` → `HE STARTS PREACHING.` → `THEY STAY AND LISTEN.`

segments.voice: First, Francis and his sisters the birds. In the Little Flowers, Francis addresses them as his little sisters. Most of his sermon isn't about their faults. He reminds them how much they've been given: feathers to wear, the air to fly in, rivers and springs to drink from, and food they never had to sow or reap. So, he tells them, beware of ingratitude, and praise your Creator. In that story, the birds aren't scenery; they're fellow creatures with their own reasons to give thanks. Second, a righteous man regardeth his beast. Proverbs puts it in one short line: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." How someone treats an animal in their care isn't a side issue; it's part of being righteous. Third, the Jain care for small lives. In the Jain tradition, ahimsa, not harming, reaches all the way down to the smallest living things. The Acaranga Sutra teaches that all beings love life and dislike pain, so none should be harmed. Some Jain monks and nuns carry a soft broom to sweep insects gently from where they're about to step or sit. Buddhists, too, place not harming living beings at the very start of their precepts. Fourth, gentleness, small and daily: slowing down for a dog on a leash, carrying a spider outside instead of crushing it, filling the water bowl before your own coffee. Francis called them sisters. That one word can change how a person walks past a pigeon.

segments.voice: Let an animal come to mind, a pet beside you, a bird outside the window, a dog from childhood, even an ant on the counter, and see it simply as a living thing, breathing too, wanting to live, avoiding pain. Then do what Francis did in the field and name its gifts silently: fur or feathers, air, water, a way of moving that belongs to it. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this creature.
Loving animals. Care that reaches past our own kind, the way Francis called the birds his sisters and the Jain path refuses to harm even the smallest life. Today's word.
Your line: sister birds. Fur, feathers and shell all count as kin. That's day eight hundred sixty-five.

866.title: The earth
866.hook: Francis calls the earth sister and mother (Canticle of the Creatures)
866.howItsDone: Christians sing and pray Francis's Canticle of the Creatures, and some churches and communities hold creation-care days, garden work and cleanups; Jews and Christians read Genesis 2 as a call to tend and keep the earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was loving animals: care that reaches past our own kind. Your line was sister birds.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. That's the cast list of a short song by Francis of Assisi, the Canticle of the Creatures. Tradition says he made it late in his life, when he was sick and his eyes were failing: a song in praise of the sun, from a man who could hardly see it. He goes through the whole family of creation, one relative at a time. Then he reaches the ground under everyone's feet, and gives it two names at once.
screen: `BROTHER SUN, SISTER MOON.` → `A WHOLE FAMILY OF CREATION.` → `TWO NAMES FOR THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: First, brother sun, sister water. In the Canticle, Francis praises God through each creature and gives each one a family name. The sun is a brother, beautiful and radiant. Water is a sister, useful, humble, precious and pure. The singer stands among the creatures as kin, not above them as owner. Second, our sister, mother earth. When Francis reaches the earth, one family word isn't enough. She's our sister, and our mother, who sustains us, governs us, and brings forth fruits and colored flowers and herbs. Sister: kin, alongside us. Mother: she feeds us. Third, to dress it and to keep it. Francis didn't invent this care. In Genesis, the first human is put in the garden of Eden with a job: "to dress it and to keep it." Tend it and guard it. And the Psalms add whose it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." In that picture, people are gardeners and keepers, not owners. Fourth, heaven under our feet. Henry David Thoreau, in Walden, writing about a pond in winter, put it this way: "Heaven is under our feet as well as over our heads." He wasn't a monk or a saint, but he arrived at a similar place: the ground is holy ground. Sister earth isn't an abstraction. It's the strip of grass by the bus stop, the window box, the park with the litter in it. Love for the earth starts with one patch of it.

segments.voice: Put your feet flat on the floor and feel your weight settle through them, down past the floor and the building to the soil, and rest your attention there for a few breaths. Then let one patch of ground you pass often come to mind, a tree pit, a yard, a roadside strip, and see it clearly, litter and all, the way a keeper would. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for the earth beneath you.
The earth. The ground that Francis called our sister and our mother, that Genesis gives people to dress and keep, and that Thoreau found heaven in. Today's word.
Your line: sister earth. Kin under your feet, and a keeper's work in your hands. Day eight hundred sixty-six, done.

867.title: Love that lets go
867.hook: sometimes love means letting someone go
867.howItsDone: People on many paths practice letting go in their own ways: Christians may entrust someone to God in prayer, Buddhist teachers speak of loosening clinging in meditation, and families mark leavings with blessings, meals or small rituals.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the earth: our sister and our mother, Francis said. Your line was sister earth.

The car is packed to the roof. A lamp, a laundry basket, a box marked kitchen in thick marker. A parent stands in a dorm hallway that smells of fresh paint, and the hardest part of the day is not the stairs. It's walking back to the car alone. Every instinct says stay one more hour, fix one more shelf. And the kid, very kindly, is already looking past them at the people down the hall. Nothing has gone wrong. This is what it looks like when everything went right.
screen: `THE CAR PACKED TO THE ROOF.` → `WALKING BACK ALONE.` → `WHEN EVERYTHING WENT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Start with a story Jesus tells in the Gospel of Luke, known as the prodigal son. Look at the beginning, not the famous ending. The younger son asks for his share of the family money early, while his father is still alive. In the King James Bible: "Father, give me the portion of goods that falleth to me. And he divided unto them his living." No lecture is recorded. No conditions. The father lets him go. Second, the waiting. When the son finally turns back, the story says the father saw him while he was "yet a great way off." Some readers notice what that suggests: he had been watching the road. In that reading, letting go didn't mean he stopped loving; he loved without holding the door shut. Third, a different shelf of the Bible. Ecclesiastes sets life out as a list of seasons, and two of its lines land right here: "a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing," and "a time to keep, and a time to cast away." The book doesn't say which time you're in, only that both are real. Fourth, Buddhist teaching has a word for the opposite of this kind of love: clinging. In the Buddha's first sermon, craving is named as the origin of suffering, and love that clings starts to squeeze. Letting go isn't coldness. It's love that has stopped needing to own. The father, the seasons, the open hand: releasing someone can be an act of love, not the end of it.

segments.voice: Let your hands rest wherever they fall, and bring to mind one person you're holding tightly right now: a child growing up, a friend moving away, someone whose choices aren't yours to make, someone who has already gone. If your hands have curled, let them rest open on your knees, and hold that person in mind with the grip eased a little, still caring. If you pray, you can place them in God's keeping in your own tradition's words.
Prodigal son. The parable where a father lets his son go, then watches the road, loving without holding the door shut. Today's word.

868.title: Love unreturned
868.hook: love that isn't returned is still love
868.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Leah's story in Genesis as scripture, and some teachers read it as a portrait of unanswered love and of a turn toward praise; Christians also read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13 as scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prodigal son: the father who divided his living and let his son go. Your line was let go, lovingly.

A text sits on a phone with one small word under it, read, and a time stamp. No reply. An hour later, still nothing. A day later, still nothing. Some loves go like that. A crush that never turned around. A parent who couldn't say it back. A friend who drifted while you kept reaching. There's a woman in the book of Genesis who lived it, and the text gives her the words to say it. Her name is Leah.
screen: `READ, AND NO REPLY.` → `SOME LOVES GO LIKE THAT.` → `A WOMAN NAMED LEAH.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Jacob loves Rachel. He works for her father to marry her, and on the wedding night the father swaps in her older sister, Leah. Jacob marries Rachel too, and Genesis says it plainly: he "loved also Rachel more than Leah." Leah lives inside a marriage where the love runs one way. Second, her words. When her first son is born, she names him and says, in the King James text: "Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." With the sons that follow, she keeps hoping out loud: that the LORD has heard her, that her husband will be joined to her. Genesis doesn't hurry past her hope. It lets her say it, son after son. Third, the turn. With another son, her words change: "Now will I praise the LORD." No mention of Jacob this time. Nothing in the story says he suddenly loves her back. What changes is where Leah stands. Her love hasn't been returned, and she sets it down, not by hating anyone, but by turning toward praise. Fourth, a line from Paul that fits her. In his letter to the Corinthians, love, which the King James Bible calls charity, "seeketh not her own." Love that isn't paid back is not a failed transaction; in Paul's description, it was never a transaction to begin with. Christians and Jews read Leah's story in their own ways, and some readers see in her a quiet strength. Either way, the text gives an unreturned love its full weight, and calls it what it was.
screen: `HE LOVED RACHEL MORE THAN LEAH.` · `NOW MY HUSBAND WILL LOVE ME.` · `NOW WILL I PRAISE THE LORD.` · `LOVE SEEKETH NOT HER OWN.` · then, large: `LOVE UNRETURNED.`

segments.voice: This week turned to parents, children, strangers, animals, the earth, and people who had to be let go; now let the breath settle, and bring to mind one love that wasn't returned, old or recent, small or large, without arguing with it or reopening the case. Say inwardly, that was love, and if anger comes, let it pass by like weather. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words.
Love unreturned. Love that went out and didn't come back, like Leah's, and still counts as love. Today's word.
Your line: still love. Unreturned isn't the same as wasted, and it never was. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.
